name_or_item: BR Mk1, all variants: heavy body on a separate load-bearing underframe, spartan finish
source_ref: Divall and Shin, 'Engineers v. industrial designers: the struggle for professional control over the British Railways Mark 2 Coach, c.1955-66', Journal of Transport History 2018, accepted version, pp.18-19, 43; https://doi.org/10.1177/0022526618768417
notes: Confidence: medium-high. Sign convention: positive = dearer to build or better regarded, applied to the fitted base price. Two forces pull opposite ways: the separate body and underframe is more labour per ton than an integral shell, but the finish was 'at best workman-like' with 'spartan fittings and predominantly wooden wall finishes', built in batch in BR's own works. The heaviness is already charged by a weight-driven ladder, so the net is -5, not a premium. Do not read this as a durability judgement; see the corrosion and crash-structure rows.

name_or_item: BR Mk1: corrosion of door pillars, window frames, gangway ends and gutters
source_ref: Bluebell Railway, 'Carriage Fleet Review 7: the Mark 1', Carriage and Wagon department, last updated 2009; https://www.bluebell-railway.co.uk/bluebell/carrev7_mk1.html
notes: Confidence: medium. Operating-department statement, but from a heritage operator in the 2000s, not BR accounts. 'The main weakness in Mk.I design being the door and door-frame structure'; end-loading pillars 'rusted almost completely through at the bottom'; each coach needs 'major work each decade'. Treat as a reliability discount, not a lower build price.

name_or_item: BR Mk1: light body on a heavy underframe in overriding collisions
source_ref: Wilson and Kirk, 'Techniques for improving the crashworthiness of existing designs of railway rolling stock', Journal de Physique IV 10 (2000), PR9; https://doi.org/10.1051/jp4:2000993
notes: Confidence: medium-high. HSE/Railway Inspectorate research: the Mk1 'basic design consists of a substantial underframe... a relatively light body is then attached'; in an override the underframe climbs and penetrates the upper body. This is why the class left the national network; it is a service-life and regulatory penalty rather than a build cost.

name_or_item: BR Mk2: integral stressed-skin body
notes: Confidence: medium-high. Integral construction 'gave a much lighter vehicle for a given strength'. Because the saving is weight, the fitted ladder already captures most of it; the residual +5 is the stress analysis, tooling and the loss of flexibility (the body was load-bearing, so door, window and gangway openings could not be moved cheaply).

name_or_item: BR Mk3: air-conditioning, secondary air suspension and 23 m body beyond what weight explains
source_ref: Rail Magazine, 'Making the Mk 3s even better', 13 June 2012; Watts, 'Mark IV Coaches for British Rail Intercity', IEE Conference on Electrification, York, September 1989; https://www.railmagazine.com/trains/current-trains/making-the-mk-3s-even-better
notes: Confidence: medium. Mk3 was the first 23 m UK coach, with BT10 bogies and secondary air suspension; APT publicity of 1980 gives a Mk III at 34 t against an aluminium APT trailer at 24 t. The +5 is for the systems, not the shell.

name_or_item: BR Mk3: BT10 axlebox fatigue and disc-brake bolt fractures, 1977-78
source_ref: Power, 'High Speed Train: fleet operation', Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers 192 (1978) No.35, Railway Division; https://www.steane.com/images/documents/IMechE/High%20Speed%20Train%20-%20Fleet%20Operation.pdf
notes: Confidence: high. Chief Mechanical and Electrical Engineer, BR Paddington, writing in 1978: 'Following discovery of a fractured axle box on a Mark III locomotive hauled coach, an immediate survey of all HST coach axleboxes was undertaken and this resulted in a number of vehicles being withdrawn'; the axlebox was redesigned. Discs on Mk3 LHCS 'began to fracture', and fractures continued.

name_or_item: BR Mk3: bodyshell corrosion and PRM non-compliance in later life
source_ref: Rail Magazine, 'Making the Mk 3s even better', 13 June 2012, quoting Dave Hogwood, Chiltern project engineer; https://www.railmagazine.com/trains/current-trains/making-the-mk-3s-even-better
notes: Confidence: medium. Chiltern's rebuild: 'beyond the doors, the major work required is to repair corrosion damage', after which coaches last 'at least 10 to 12 years before the work is required again'. The same article records that rebuilding is cheaper than new DMUs, which is evidence the vehicles are durable despite corrosion.

name_or_item: BR Mk4: new-design risk at introduction, 1989-1991
source_ref: British Railways Board, 'Electrification of the East Coast Main Line: Project Completion Certificate', 1992, project director's letter, via Railways Archive; https://www.railwaysarchive.co.uk/documents/BRB_ECMLCompletion1992.pdf
notes: Confidence: medium-high. The project director: 'the decision to go for new designs in both the power units and the coaches was high risk and, as the progress reports from October 1988 onwards show, we paid the price.' New bodyshell, new bogies (SIG BT41) and new gangways in one step.

name_or_item: Pullman and dining cars: catering fittings, low-volume hand finish and heavy tare
source_ref: Pullman Car Services archive, car history sheets (SREmG), cars MADELINE and GSR 100-103; https://sremg.org.uk/coach/coupe/pull_ciwl-news051.pdf
notes: Confidence: medium. Measured ratio: a 1926 Pullman kitchen car cost GBP5,050 against GBP2,300-2,500 for a 1924-30 corridor third, so about 2.0-2.2 times. The whole of that gap should not go into a class term: kitchen equipment is a separate object in the pakset and the low volume inflates the unit price. +15 is the defensible part.

name_or_item: Pullman kitchen car MADELINE, Metropolitan-Cammell, 20 seats, 39 t tare, 57 ft 1.5 in
source_ref: Pullman Car Services archive (SREmG), 'Pullman Car History: Madeline', https://sremg.org.uk/coach/coupe/pull_ciwl-news051.pdf, accessed 2026-11-22
notes: Confidence: medium-high. Car record states 'Cost: GBP5,050.00', builder, tare, seating and length. Archive compiled by A. Ford from Pullman Car Company records.

name_or_item: Pullman third-class buffet cars 100-103 for the Great Southern Railway of Ireland, Birmingham RC&W, 46 seats, 39.5 t
source_ref: Pullman Car Services archive (SREmG), 'The Irish Third-Class Pullman Cars', https://sremg.org.uk/coach/coupe/pull_ciwl-news055.pdf, accessed 2026-11-22
notes: Confidence: medium-high. 'The cost of each car at GBP5,537.25 was at the PCCo expense' under the agreement of 18 April 1925. Sold to GSR in 1937 at GBP1,499 each, which is a second-hand value ten years on.

name_or_item: Pullman 12-wheel kitchen third No. 53: 1929 conversion cost
source_ref: Pullman Car Services archive (SREmG), 'Pullman Car History: Third Class Car No. 53', https://sremg.org.uk/coach/coupe/pull_ciwl-news035.pdf, accessed 2026-11-22
notes: Confidence: medium-high. Stated as 'GBP471.3.9' for conversion to a first-class restaurant car with 18 dining seats and two pantries. A refit figure, not a build figure; useful as a lower bound on catering conversion.

name_or_item: Pullman/dining premium measured: 1926 Pullman kitchen car against 1924-30 corridor third
source_ref: Pullman archive as above; NER/ SR corridor third prices from vehicle-cost/forum-prices-part-1.md rows in the knowledge base; https://sremg.org.uk/coach/coupe/pull_ciwl-news051.pdf
notes: Confidence: medium. GBP5,050 against GBP2,300-2,500 = 2.02 to 2.20. Different years, builders and diagrams, so the ratio is an order of magnitude, not a measurement. Do not enter 102 per cent as a class term.

name_or_item: Pre-grouping and Big Four carriage price relatives: no new adjustment recommended
source_ref: Knowledge base rows already hold the NER, Midland, GWR and Highland same-body pairs: vehicle-cost/forum-prices-part-1.md, summarised in research-pricing-report-8.md S5
notes: Confidence: high that nothing new is needed. The existing pairs (six-wheel against bogie +19.4 per cent; steel against wood panelling +25 per cent; first against third +78.4 per cent; clerestory +2.6 per cent) already separate body, bogie and finish. Adding a second, weaker class term here would double-count.

name_or_item: BR 16-ton all-steel mineral wagon, diagrams 1/108 and relatives
source_ref: British Railways, 'Facts and Figures about British Railways', 1956 edition, pp.22-23; English Braille and Midland Railway Society, 'British Railways mineral wagons 1945 to 1962'; LTSV rail data profile 41; https://my1950s.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/BR-1956-OCR.pdf
notes: Confidence: medium-high. 352,801 built to 1962 by 28 builders in 183 lots, 206,444 to diagram 1/108 alone; 42,000 built in 1955 alone. 'By standardisation it has been possible to reduce the number of designs in current production.' Cheap because of volume and because it is unsprung, unfitted and has no brake other than Morton gear.

name_or_item: BR 16-ton mineral wagon: short economic life and early withdrawal
source_ref: British Railways, 'Facts and Figures about British Railways', 1959 edition, pp.20-23; https://my1950s.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/br-1959.pdf
notes: Confidence: medium-high. 121,000 wagons withdrawn in 1958 against 36,284 built; the 16-ton orders were 'almost complete' and future coal stock was to be over 20 tons. A wagon class designed for a 40-year life was being displaced within ten years of the end of its build, which is a durability signal the ladder does not carry.

name_or_item: Private owner coal wagons: cheap specification, neglect and short life
source_ref: Gloucester Railway Carriage and Wagon Company records via Gloucestershire Archives, 'Universal Works' page, C.P. Teague fleet; igg.org.uk, 'British Private Owner Wagon and Van Design'; https://glostransporthistory.visit-gloucestershire.co.uk/ROD_Universal%20Works_GA_GRCW.html
notes: Confidence: medium. A c.1906 Gloucester-built PO wagon cost GBP66 against GBP81 for a 10-ton railway-owned Shildon wagon of 1906, so about 18 per cent cheaper. PO wagons were 'often poorly maintained', with grease axleboxes that 'dried out, causing fires and sometimes melting the ends off the axles'. The 1919 Ministry of Transport power to restrict them was never used.

name_or_item: Vacuum-fitted stock: the minority of the fleet and the dearer option
source_ref: British Railways, 'Facts and Figures about British Railways', 1956 edition, p.23; https://my1950s.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/BR-1956-OCR.pdf
notes: Confidence: medium-high. Only 178,033 of about 1,125,000 freight wagons were fitted at the end of 1955, and the pipe-fitted share of carrying stock was 21 per cent. Fitting is a real cost premium: brake cylinder, train pipe, couplings and maintenance. Applies to fitted wagons as a class, not to individual diagrams.

name_or_item: Private owner 7-plank coal wagon, Gloucester RCW, C.P. Teague fleet
scope: complete wagon, no vacuum brake, grease axleboxes
source_ref: Gloucester Railway Carriage and Wagon Company records via Gloucestershire Archives, 'Universal Works', https://glostransporthistory.visit-gloucestershire.co.uk/ROD_Universal%20Works_GA_GRCW.html, accessed 2026-11-22
notes: Confidence: medium. 'Wagon 6 was purchased for GBP66.00 and the original seven year repair contract with GRCW was renewed in October 1913.' The exact build year is not stated; Teague bought from 1906 and wagon 7 followed in October 1907, so c.1906-07. Sold with a seven-year repair contract, which is itself a maintenance-cost fact.

name_or_item: Private owner wagon compensation at nationalisation: 8-ton wagon
source_ref: igg.org.uk, 'British Private Owner Wagon and Van Design', http://igg.org.uk/rail/4-rstock/powag1.htm, accessed 2026-11-22
notes: Confidence: low-medium. 'Sixteen pound ten shillings for an 8-ton Private Owner wagon', paid 'regardless of condition'. A scrap-value proxy for a worn-out wagon, not a build price. Treat as the bottom of the range, not as evidence of new cost.

name_or_item: Freightliner expansion 1968: containers and flats together
scope: 4,750 containers plus 875 Freightliner wagons, equipment only
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 'New GBP12.5m expansion of BR Freightliner services', 10 May 1968, p.23; https://archive.commercialmotor.com/article/10th-may-1968/23/n-ew-12m-expansion-of-br-freightliner-services
notes: Confidence: medium. 'Some 4,750 containers and 875 Freightliner wagons are needed... The total cost of the equipment will be about GBP8m.' The source does not split wagons from containers, so no per-wagon figure can be derived without an assumption. Recorded as an upper bound only.

name_or_item: First-generation DMUs: design weaknesses and availability, 1954-1971
source_ref: British Transport Commission, 'Multiple Unit Diesel Trains: memorandum of meeting held at Marylebone, 14 February 1955', via railcar.co.uk; Wakefield, 'Twenty years' experience with diesel railcars', IMechE Railway Division, paper RDP 2/71, 1971; https://www.railcar.co.uk/topic/archive/55-02-14/
notes: Confidence: high. The 1955 memo records 'the deterioration which had occurred in the availability of the West Riding Diesel Trains'; the troubles 'could not be attributed to faulty workmanship either in Railway Workshops or by Contractors', so they were design, not build. Wakefield's 1971 paper is '19 pages of problems', and he says mistakes 'were obviously made in many areas'.

name_or_item: First-generation DMUs: underfloor engine fire risk
source_ref: Discussion contribution by J.R.H. Robertson, in Wakefield, RDP 2/71, 1971, reported in SteamIndex summary of Journal of the Institution of Locomotive Engineers 1967-69; https://steamindex.com/jile/rdj.htm
notes: Confidence: medium-high. Fires in underfloor equipment of DMU power cars peaked at 57 in 1965 and were 42 in 1969; the rate rose from about 0.6 per 100 power cars in 1961 to about 2.5 in 1965 and was still 2.07 in 1969. About 1.2 million miles per fire. 'Extensive and expensive series of modifications' were needed.

name_or_item: Southern Region diesel-electric multiple units: body-mounted engines
source_ref: J.R.H. Robertson, discussion in Wakefield RDP 2/71, 1971; https://steamindex.com/jile/rdj.htm
notes: Confidence: medium-high. Direct comparison by a contemporary engineer: 'the outstandingly good fire record of the diesel-electric multiple-unit trains of Southern Region which had body-mounted engines'. A like-for-like statement about a design choice, which is the sort of evidence this adjustment layer needs.

name_or_item: Pacer family, Classes 141-144: bus body on a four-wheel wagon underframe
source_ref: Rail Magazine, 'From the archives: Pacers, the unlikely local heroes', 26 August 2019 (RAIL 857); Zavanak, 'The Class 142 Pacers', 24 June 2021, from Leyland and BREL documents; https://www.railmagazine.com/news/rail-features/pacers-the-unlikely-local-heroes-2
notes: Confidence: medium. Measured: a Class 142 two-car set cost GBP340,000 in January 1984 against GBP481 per vehicle implied by the Sprinter order (GBP149.5m for 568 vehicles, 1984-86), so about 35 per cent cheaper per vehicle. The reliability record is separately poor: 26 of 57 Newton Heath Class 142s out of service in July 1987; the whole Class 143 fleet affected; all three classes later re-engined and re-transmissioned.

name_or_item: Pacer family: ride, track wear and crew health penalties
source_ref: Zavanak, 'The Class 142 Pacers', 2021, citing a confidential BR study of the early 1990s; Rail Magazine, 26 August 2019; https://zavanak.com/transport-topics/the-class-142-pacers/
notes: Confidence: low-medium. Both sources are secondary. The mechanism is documented: no bogies, so excessive track and tyre wear on curves, and a driving cab far ahead of the wheels amplifying pitch. Pacers were barred from some routes for gradient and curve reasons. A real cost, but not one the pakset charges.

name_or_item: Sprinter family, Classes 150/155/156: conventional bogie DMU
source_ref: Rail Magazine, 'The Class 150 Sprinter 40 years on', 23 August 2024; https://www.railmagazine.com/features-1/the-class-150-sprinter-40-years-on
notes: Confidence: medium. GBP149.5m for 568 vehicles, GBP263,204 each at 1984-86 prices, against GBP170,000 for a Class 142 car. Dearer per vehicle and 'consistently less reliable' is the Pacer's record, not the Sprinter's: the Sprinters are the benchmark the Pacers are measured against.

name_or_item: PEP family, Classes 313/314/315/507/508: aluminium-alloy integral body, all axles motored
source_ref: Railway Magazine archive, 'First batch of class 508 electric multiple-units in service', March 1980, republished 18 March 2020; Modern Railways, 'Cross-Southern Country', 21 November 2019; Railway Magazine, 'Multiple unit stalwart: dual-voltage pioneers', 17 July 2017; https://www.railwaymagazine.co.uk/14150/from-the-archive-first-batch-of-class-508-electric-multiple-units-in-service/
notes: Confidence: medium-high. Lightweight aluminium-alloy and steel integral body; a 508 trailer weighs 26.5 t against a Class 450 trailer at 35.5 t. The PEP was 'a great machine' with 'terrific acceleration'. Class 313s ran from 1976 to 2023 and Class 507s from 1978 into the mid-2020s, which is the durability evidence.

name_or_item: Class 508 on the Southern Region: braking and wheel-slide trouble
source_ref: Key Model World, 'British Rail PEP electric multiple unit story', 28 July 2023; Railway Magazine archive, March 1980; https://www.keymodelworld.com/article/british-rail-pep-electric-multiple-unit-story
notes: Confidence: low-medium. The 508s 'didn't find much favour with the operating department, which had issues with braking and wheel slide, with one unit failing to stop at Shepperton station and running through the buffer stops'. They were moved to Merseyrail as soon as Class 455s were available. A class-specific penalty inside an otherwise good family.

name_or_item: Class 455: value-engineered Mk3-derived EMU, 25 per cent of axles motored
source_ref: Modern Railways, 'Cross-Southern Country', 21 November 2019; https://www.modernrailways.com/article/cross-southern-country
notes: Confidence: medium. Contemporary engineering account: the 508s were 'value engineered' from the PEP with motored axles cut from 100 to 50 per cent, and the 455 went to 25 per cent with a steel body 'roughly based on the Mk 3 coach'. Cheaper to build and slower, which the pakset's power and weight fields already capture in part.

name_or_item: Class 508 four-car set, BREL York, 43 sets
source_ref: Railway Magazine archive, 'First batch of class 508 electric multiple-units in service', March 1980, republished 18 March 2020, https://www.railwaymagazine.co.uk/14150/, accessed 2026-11-22
notes: Confidence: high. 'GBP26m for the 43 four-car sets' = GBP604,651 per set, GBP151,163 per vehicle. Contemporary magazine, stated contract total and vehicle count, no scope ambiguity beyond 'built at York Works'.

name_or_item: Class 141 two-car set, Leyland body and BREL assembly, 20 sets
source_ref: Zavanak, 'The Class 142 Pacers', 24 June 2021, https://zavanak.com/transport-topics/the-class-142-pacers/, accessed 2026-11-22, from Leyland and BREL documents
notes: Confidence: medium. 'The price was just GBP8 million - GBP400,000 per two-car unit' = GBP200,000 per vehicle. Secondary source, but the arithmetic and the fleet size are consistent with the Class 142 figure below.

name_or_item: Class 142 two-car set, January 1984 order for 50
source_ref: Zavanak, 'The Class 142 Pacers', 2021, from Leyland and BREL documents; Rail Magazine, 26 August 2019 for the fleet and reliability record; https://steamindex.com/jile/rdj.htm
notes: Confidence: medium. '50 Class 142 sets worth GBP17 million or GBP340,000 per set' = GBP170,000 per vehicle. The same source compares this with an estimated GBP1m for a three-car Class 210, 'almost half the price on a car by car basis'.

name_or_item: Sprinter order: Classes 150/2, 155 and 156, 568 vehicles
source_ref: Rail Magazine, 'The Class 150 Sprinter 40 years on', 23 August 2024, https://www.railmagazine.com/features-1/the-class-150-sprinter-40-years-on, accessed 2026-11-22
notes: Confidence: medium-high. 'In total, the order for these 568 vehicles came in at GBP149.5 million.' Derived per-vehicle figure GBP263,204. Mixed classes and mixed build dates 1984-86, so treat as a family average, not a class price.

name_or_item: First-generation DMU fleet maintenance, 1969
scope: maintenance only, whole fleet, per mile
source_ref: Wakefield, 'Twenty years' experience with diesel railcars', RDP 2/71, 1971, quoted in SteamIndex summary of the Journal of the Institution of Locomotive Engineers; https://steamindex.com/jile/rdj.htm
notes: Confidence: medium. 'The total cost of maintaining the existing fleet of these vehicles in 1969 was GBP11.8m and during that time the total train mileage was 62.2m: giving an average cost of maintenance of GBP0.19 per vehicle mile.' The arithmetic (11.8/62.2 = 0.1897) works only on train miles, so the stated 'vehicle mile' is probably wrong. Record the figure, do not propagate the unit.
